blocks.text: Task: Future exercise: finish the Day 2 checklist, then build the evidence in this book. Reading this draft does not mean tests or benchmarks have run.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Separate the subjects

A unit test calls a small C++ API in-process. An integration test launches opt and checks plugin loading, registration, scheduling, and output. A differential test compares program observations. A benchmark measures cost after correctness checks. A table of statistics alone is none of these assertions.
Step 2 — Make failures local

items: One negative fixture should isolate one rejection reason; avoid adding EH and block addresses to the same reason test.
One branch test should exercise both destinations. One switch test should include every case and default.
Store intentional source fixtures under tests/. Keep generated IR, executables, reports, and temporary logs under build/.

blocks.text: Step 3 — Keep a support matrix

Feature                  Expected decision        Evidence to add
ordinary conditional     accept                   both outcomes
loop-carried PHI         accept after preparation zero/one/many iterations
switch/shared targets    accept                   cases + default
non-static alloca        reject before mutation   reason + unchanged IR
EH/coroutine/blockaddr   reject before mutation   isolated valid fixtures
Verify
For each row, write down the expected outcome before running the implementation. An expectation generated by the same broken algorithm is not an independent oracle.

blocks.title: Well-formedness and refinement are different claims

blocks.text: A verifier checks LLVM structural rules such as type agreement, terminator placement, and dominance. A true/false destination swap can satisfy all those rules and still change a result. Equivalence work must also account for the defined input domain and observable effects; undefined behavior can make a naive comparison meaningless.
Read the [LLVM testing guide](https://llvm.org/docs/TestingGuide.html) for the distinction between regression infrastructure and tests of behavior.
Checkpoint: Which test would catch a wrong state constant that still names an existing block?
LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
Use one complete example to separate structural and behavioral claims before building tests.
What changes: PHI transport and branch routing change, while both original outcomes must be preserved.

  store i32 %ms.next, ptr %ms.state, align 4

left:                                             ; preds = %ms.dispatch

  store i32 2, ptr %ms.state, align 4

The template to start with

add_library(MiniShieldCore STATIC # TODO: implementation sources)
add_library(MiniShield MODULE lib/Plugin.cpp)
# TODO: PIC, usage requirements, LLVM linkage, and tests.
Step 1 — Move only your implementation sources

Keep Plugin.cpp in the MODULE target. Put the pass, analysis, eligibility, and completed builder implementations in MiniShieldCore. This archive contains your object files; it is not a second static build of LLVM.
Step 2 — Propagate required headers and linkage

The core headers expose LLVM types, so clients need the include paths and definitions. PUBLIC propagates those usage requirements to the plugin and tests. Link the imported shared LLVM target. Set POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE on the static core because its objects will enter a shared module.
Step 3 — Register GoogleTest with CTest

Use the installed package, not a network download. GTest::gtest_main supplies main(). include(CTest) enables BUILD_TESTING; discovery turns TEST macros into individually selectable CTest entries. This draft raises the minimum to CMake 3.20 for the later ctest --test-dir examples.
The full CMake reference

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(MiniShield CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)
set(LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB ON)
find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)
separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})

add_library(MiniShieldCore STATIC
    lib/FlatteningPass.cpp lib/StatsPass.cpp lib/CFGAnalyzer.cpp
    lib/FunctionEligibility.cpp lib/StateMachineBuilder.cpp)
set_target_properties(MiniShieldCore PROPERTIES POSITION_INDEPENDENT_CODE ON)
target_compile_definitions(MiniShieldCore PUBLIC ${MS_LLVM_DEFS})
target_include_directories(MiniShieldCore PUBLIC
    ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS} ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_link_libraries(MiniShieldCore PUBLIC LLVM)

add_library(MiniShield MODULE lib/Plugin.cpp)
target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE MiniShieldCore)

    LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR})

include(CTest)

    find_package(GTest CONFIG REQUIRED)
    add_executable(minishield-unit tests/unit/CoreTest.cpp)
    target_link_libraries(minishield-unit PRIVATE MiniShieldCore GTest::gtest_main)

blocks.title: Translation units, archives, and one definition

blocks.text: Each .cpp becomes a translation unit and then an object file. A static archive packages those objects for the linker. Avoid also listing the same implementation .cpp directly in every consuming target: duplicated definitions, especially a second AnalysisKey definition in one linked image, can break linkage or identity assumptions. A header declaration does not replace the single out-of-line definition.
Checkpoint: Which target supplies the plugin entry point, and which supplies CFGAnalyzer::Key?

blocks.title: Link-time lookup and runtime lookup are different

blocks.text: LIBRARY_PATH helps the compiler driver locate libraries while linking. It does not tell the Linux loader where to find a shared GoogleTest at execution time. The reference gives the unit executable a BUILD_RPATH using imported target directories so gtest discovery can execute it during the build. This is a build-tree setting; installation/relocation needs its own policy. A loader failure before any TEST executes is an infrastructure failure, not an LLVM assertion.
Checkpoint: Why can linking succeed while gtest_discover_tests fails to launch the executable?
References: [CMake GoogleTest integration](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/module/GoogleTest.html) and [add_test](https://cmake.org/cmake/help/latest/command/add_test.html).
Checkpoint: Why does PIC belong on the static core even though that target is not itself a shared library?

blocks.title: RAII, unique_ptr, and reverse destruction order

blocks.text: RAII binds cleanup to object lifetime. module owns its Module through unique_ptr; getFunction returns a borrowed pointer, not a second owner. Local objects are destroyed in reverse construction order: declaring context first and module second makes the module die before its context. Returning a module tied to a context created inside parse would leave a dangling dependency.

llvm::LLVMContext context;       // created first, destroyed last
auto module = parse(context, diamond); // owns Module
auto *function = module->getFunction("choose"); // borrows Function
// Do not delete function or wrap it in an owning unique_ptr.

blocks.text: Task: Future exercise: append the graph test to CoreTest.cpp. Follow the same parse → verify → run → assert pattern.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Register the dependencies

CFGAnalyzer asks FAM for dominator and loop analyses. PassBuilder::registerFunctionAnalyses installs standard function analyses; registerPass adds your custom one. This test requests function analyses directly. A module pipeline needs the corresponding outer managers and proxy registration; do not blindly transplant this minimal harness into a module pipeline.
Step 2 — Predict the graph

The diamond has four blocks, four edges, no natural loop, and no back edge. Entry dominates all its reachable blocks. Predecessor enumeration order is not an invariant; compare sets/counts when order is irrelevant.
Step 3 — Check relationships, not labels

Name-based lookup is acceptable for a hand-written input fixture, but a transformation test should usually discover its new dispatcher from edges and instruction kinds. LLVM can suffix names to avoid collisions.
The full graph test
Extend it

items: Add a natural loop fixture and identify the header/latch pointers. Check that the header dominates the latch and that the recorded edge is latch → header.
Add an unreachable cycle to ensure the reachable-back-edge rule does not count it as an entry-reachable natural loop.
Keep loop count separate from back-edge count: several latches may belong to one loop.

blocks.title: Analysis caching and borrowed result lifetimes

blocks.text: getResult returns a reference to a cached result owned by the manager. const auto& avoids copying that result but does not freeze the IR. After a transform, invalidation may destroy or replace the cache. Do not retain the old CFG reference across mutation and then assume it describes the new graph. Returning PreservedAnalyses::all() after rewriting would falsely claim such caches remain valid.
See [Using the New Pass Manager](https://llvm.org/docs/NewPassManager.html) for manager registration and invalidation.

The template to start with

Step 1 — Define what is observable

This pure function driver prints a result and returns zero. Compare stdout bytes, stderr bytes, and exit status. Require zero success before accepting equality: two crashes or two usage errors must fail. Programs with files, time, randomness, or external side effects require a richer controlled oracle.
Step 2 — Fix the domain and seed

amount is −1000 through 10000 and level is 0 through 5. The bounded multiplication stays within int range. Boundary cases ensure small inputs and default switch paths are always tested. A dedicated Random(seed) produces repeatable cases within this Python environment; persist the actual failing case as a regression rather than relying on cross-version PRNG guarantees.
Step 3 — Bound subprocess execution

Pass an argument list without shell=True. A timeout is a failing observation, not proof of an infinite loop. Report seed, index, arguments, both observations, and tool versions. These known drivers produce small output; an untrusted or noisy workload would also need output limits.
The full runner reference

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import argparse
import random
import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("original", type=Path)
parser.add_argument("protected", type=Path)
parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=20261112)
parser.add_argument("--samples", type=int, default=100)
args = parser.parse_args()
if args.samples < 0:
    parser.error("--samples must be nonnegative")
programs = [str(args.original.resolve()), str(args.protected.resolve())]
rng = random.Random(args.seed)
cases = [(a, level) for a in (-1000, -1, 0, 1, 99, 100, 10000)
         for level in range(6)]
cases += [(rng.randint(-1000, 10000), rng.randint(0, 5))
          for _ in range(args.samples)]

def run(program, case):
    result = subprocess.run([program, *map(str, case)],
                            capture_output=True, timeout=3, check=False)
    return result.returncode, result.stdout, result.stderr

for index, case in enumerate(cases):
    try:
        left, right = (run(program, case) for program in programs)
    except (subprocess.TimeoutExpired, OSError) as error:
        raise SystemExit(f"FAIL seed={args.seed} index={index} case={case}: {error}")
    if left[0] != 0 or right[0] != 0 or left != right:
        raise SystemExit(f"FAIL seed={args.seed} index={index} case={case}\n"
                         f"original={left!r}\nprotected={right!r}")

lessons.summary: Connect unit discovery and plugin verification to one command without hiding stale builds or absent tests.
lessons.takeaway: CTest runs registered tests; it does not replace configuration and compilation.

blocks.text: Task: Future exercise: add integration registration inside the CMake BUILD_TESTING block after your unit tests work.
The template to start with

# TODO: locate opt from the configured LLVM installation.
# TODO: one plugin verification test per tracked tests/ir/*.ll fixture.
# TODO: Python runner registration only once its artifacts are buildable.
Step 1 — Use the configured plugin target path

$<TARGET_FILE:MiniShield> is evaluated by CMake for the actual output library. It avoids hardcoding a .so name or guessing an output directory. Find opt in LLVM_TOOLS_BINARY_DIR so the tests do not silently load the plugin into another LLVM release.
Step 2 — Register all tracked fixtures

The following tests launch opt and require successful parsing, loading, pipeline execution, and verification. They do not assert every rejection reason or behavioral result; those remain separate tests. CONFIGURE_DEPENDS lets CMake notice added fixtures when checking the build system.
The full integration registration

find_program(MS_OPT NAMES opt HINTS "${LLVM_TOOLS_BINARY_DIR}"
             NO_DEFAULT_PATH REQUIRED)
file(GLOB MS_IR_INPUTS CONFIGURE_DEPENDS
     "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/ir/*.ll")
foreach(input IN LISTS MS_IR_INPUTS)
    get_filename_component(stem "${input}" NAME_WE)
    add_test(NAME "IR.${stem}" COMMAND "${MS_OPT}"
        "-load-pass-plugin=$<TARGET_FILE:MiniShield>"
        "-passes=function(minishield-flatten),verify"
        -disable-output "${input}")
    set_tests_properties("IR.${stem}" PROPERTIES TIMEOUT 10)
endforeach()
Step 3 — Build the differential artifacts explicitly

             NO_DEFAULT_PATH REQUIRED)
set(MS_DIFF "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/differential")
set(MS_KERNEL "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/cases/discount.c")
set(MS_DRIVER "${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/tests/cases/discount_driver.c")
add_custom_command(
    OUTPUT "${MS_DIFF}/original" "${MS_DIFF}/protected"
    BYPRODUCTS "${MS_DIFF}/common.ll" "${MS_DIFF}/protected.ll"
    COMMAND "${CMAKE_COMMAND}" -E make_directory "${MS_DIFF}"
    COMMAND "${MS_CLANG}" -O0 -Xclang -disable-O0-optnone -S -emit-llvm
        "${MS_KERNEL}" -o "${MS_DIFF}/common.ll"
    COMMAND "${MS_OPT}" "-load-pass-plugin=$<TARGET_FILE:MiniShield>"
        "-passes=function(minishield-flatten),verify" -S
        "${MS_DIFF}/common.ll" -o "${MS_DIFF}/protected.ll"
    COMMAND "${MS_CLANG}" -O2 "${MS_DRIVER}" "${MS_DIFF}/common.ll"
        -o "${MS_DIFF}/original"
    COMMAND "${MS_CLANG}" -O2 "${MS_DRIVER}" "${MS_DIFF}/protected.ll"
        -o "${MS_DIFF}/protected"
    DEPENDS MiniShield "${MS_KERNEL}" "${MS_DRIVER}"
    VERBATIM)
add_custom_target(minishield-differential-artifacts ALL
    DEPENDS "${MS_DIFF}/original" "${MS_DIFF}/protected")

    COMMAND "${Python3_EXECUTABLE}"

        "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/differential/original"
        "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/differential/protected"

Step 3 — Shrink while preserving meaning

lessons.originalTitle: Design measurements before writing a timing loop
lessons.summary: Choose workloads, artifact boundaries, and a fair comparison that answer an actual question.
lessons.takeaway: Measure final artifacts under a recorded pipeline; do not invent expected numbers.

blocks.text: Task: Future exercise: design a small benchmark matrix after correctness checks pass. No performance measurements have been supplied by this draft.
The template to start with
Step 1 — Freeze the comparison

Use identical source, common frontend IR, target, backend optimization, driver, and input sequence. Transform only the selected kernel module. Record tool versions, commit, CPU, OS, build flags, and exact pass placement. Comparing an O0 original to an O2 protected executable is not the intended experiment.
Step 2 — Choose metrics with units

items: Runtime: median elapsed seconds or nanoseconds per call from a repeated in-process workload, with repeat count and dispersion.
Code size: total file bytes and, when available, .text bytes; keep these separate from total process memory.
IR shape: block/instruction counts before flattening, immediately after, and after final optimization. Static counts do not equal executed operations.

blocks.text: Step 3 — Inspect what survived optimization

Later LLVM passes may simplify the dispatcher, alter spill loads/stores, or inline a kernel under LTO. Inspect final optimized IR/disassembly. Report that the structure was removed when it was; matching behavior alone does not establish persistent obfuscation.

The template to start with
Step 1 — Make arithmetic and work explicit

uint32_t arithmetic wraps modulo 2^32. All shift counts here are within 0..31, and rounds is fixed at 100. A changing state and printed checksum make computed results observable. This is a small synthetic workload, not a general predictor of application performance.
The full kernel reference
Step 2 — Keep the driver outside the transformed module

Step 2 — Attach enough evidence

runtime_change_percent = 100 * (protected_seconds / original_seconds - 1)
size_change_percent = 100 * (protected_bytes / original_bytes - 1)

Question and scope

Interpretation and sources of noise

Step 1 — Classify the symptom

Ask whether the failure is an opt crash, verifier error, target crash, timeout, or wrong result. Capture the original/protected commands and confirm the original execution is defined. Reproduce on the pinned toolchain before assuming the customer’s last optimizer pass caused the defect.

Did any non-entry allocation or unsupported special instruction escape preflight?

blocks.text: Step 3 — Add a durable regression

Retain the minimized fixture and observable mismatch, assert the earliest relevant invariant, and rerun related tests. Re-measure after a correctness fix if it changes code or the accepted workload. Do not “fix” a reproducible bug solely by forcing O0.

  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %header
    i32 1, label %body
    i32 2, label %exit
  ]

ms.invalid:                                       ; preds = %ms.dispatch
  unreachable
}

Both listings are complete LLVM modules defining the example function, not fragments with omitted blocks. They have no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify them, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. These listings were generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.
Follow the values and edges: If a reduced case retains an old header-defined cross-block use, verify immediately after the pass rather than blaming the later optimizer first.
